lesson.title: The Slanted Exception: Oblique Asymptotes
lesson.summary: When a rational function's numerator has exactly one more degree than its denominator, the graph does not level off horizontally but instead approaches a slanted line, found by polynomial long division.
lesson.body:
The horizontal asymptote rule leaves a gap: when the degree of the numerator exceeds the degree of the denominator, there is no horizontal asymptote, since the function grows without bound rather than leveling off. But there is an important special case within that gap. When the numerator's degree is exactly one more than the denominator's degree, the graph does not settle to a constant height, yet it also does not diverge chaotically. Instead it approaches a slanted line as x runs toward positive or negative infinity, called an oblique asymptote, sometimes called a slant asymptote.

To find it, perform polynomial long division of the numerator by the denominator. Writing f(x) = p(x)/q(x), division gives p(x) = q(x) times (mx + b), plus a remainder r(x) whose degree is smaller than the degree of q(x), so that f(x) = mx + b + r(x)/q(x). Because the remainder's degree is smaller than the denominator's degree, the remainder term r(x)/q(x) behaves exactly like the degree(numerator) less than degree(denominator) case from horizontal asymptotes, and it approaches 0 as x approaches positive or negative infinity. That leaves f(x) getting arbitrarily close to the line y = mx + b, which is the oblique asymptote.

For a worked example, take f(x) = (x^2 + 1)/x. Dividing gives x^2 + 1 = x times x, plus a remainder of 1, so f(x) = x + 1/x. As x approaches infinity, 1/x approaches 0, so f(x) approaches x, meaning the graph gets closer and closer to the line y = x. The same holds as x approaches negative infinity, since 1/x still approaches 0. So y = x is the oblique asymptote of this function.

A numerical check confirms how close the fit becomes: at x = 100, f(100) = (10000 + 1)/100 = 100.01, extremely close to the line's value of 100 at that same x. At x = 1000, f(1000) = (1000000 + 1)/1000 = 1000.001, an even smaller relative gap. Notice also that x = 0 is excluded from the domain, since the denominator is zero there while the numerator equals 1, a nonzero value, so x = 0 is a vertical asymptote of this same function. That shows how one rational function's graph can combine a vertical asymptote with an oblique one rather than a horizontal one.

Oblique asymptotes occur only when the numerator's degree exceeds the denominator's degree by exactly one. If the gap between the degrees is two or more, the quotient from long division is no longer linear, so the graph diverges in a more complex, non-asymptotic way, following a parabola or higher-degree curve instead of a straight line. For instance, dividing x^3 by x gives a quadratic quotient x^2, which grows far faster than any straight line could match, so no oblique asymptote exists in that case. Together, the three asymptote types, vertical, horizontal, and oblique, along with this degree-difference rule, give a complete way to predict both the local breaks and the long-run shape of any rational function's graph directly from its algebra.
